newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ under pressure on rates but seen holding back.
newsitem.headline: BOJ under pressure on rates but seen holding back.

text.p: The Bank of Japan (BOJ) is coming under growing pressure to raise interest rates as the nation's economic recovery seems fairly robust, but analysts expect policymakers to bide their time for now.

Quoted comments from a senior BOJ official suggesting that the central bank may be in the process of planning a rate increase caused a stir in the markets on Wednesday but the bank later insisted it had no immediate plans for a credit-tightening.
BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita also said the current low interest rate policy was revitalising the economy, pouring cold water on speculation of an early rise in rates.
A BOJ official also said reported comments by Deputy-Governor Toshihiko Fukui on Wednesday that the bank is considering the timing for a rise in the official discount rate were misquoted.
Fukui had been quoted by a labour union official as making the comment at a meeting with union leaders in which the labour representatives urged the bank to raise rates.
The quoted comments caused heavy bond selling, pushing up Japanese government bond (JGB) yields. The yield of the key 3.0 percent 182nd 10-year JGB jumped more than 10 basis points to 2.605 percent.

Analysts said that the BOJ was likely to take a cautious approach to raising rates, despite signs that Japan's economic recovery will not be thrown off track by a rise in the national consumption tax in April.
"It is not the time yet to raise rates," said Toshikini Kaneki, economist at Sumitomo Trust and Banking.

Mineko Sasaki-Smith, chief economist at CS First Boston, said: "It was only on Monday that (BOJ research director Masayuki) Matsushima said the impact of the consumption tax hike would last three months, which gives the impression that they want to ensure the impact has disappeared before acting."

Pressure has been mounting on the BOJ to rethink its credit policy in order to help people living on interest income from their savings, and to stop too much money from flowing abroad as Japan eases rules on its financial markets.
Ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) officials have been calling for higher rates out of fear that liberalisation of the foreign exchange laws next April will trigger a damaging outflow of capital.
On Tuesday, media reports said an LDP panel will recommend to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto by the end of May that Japan raise the discount rate.
Hashimoto, however, said on Wednesday the LDP would not request a rate rise. He told a parliamentary committee it was not proper for politicians to comment on interest rates.
The discount rate, charged on BOJ loans to commercial banks, has been kept at a record low 0.5 percent since September 8, 1995 to sustain the economic recovery.

LDP Secretary-General Koichi Kato said last week that Japan may face pressure to change its current low interest rates as it opens up its financial markets to foreign competition with "Big Bang" deregulation measures.
Captains of industry have also been sounding a warning about continued low rates.

Shoichiro Toyoda, chairman of Japan's Federation of Economic Organisations, said last week that Japanese interest rates should not remain at the present levels, which had caused hardship for depositors.
"It appears that the number of people who feel the benefit from the low interest rates has declined drastically recently," said a senior manager at a Japanese long-term credit bank.
Individual depositors in Japan have been actively buying high-yielding foreign bonds to avoid parking money in low-yielding investment vehicles being offered domestically.

Asked about the chances of a Japanese interest rate rise, strategist Kenneth Landon of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said: "I think at this point it's not likely until later in the year at the earliest. The fact is that among some politicians higher rates are politically popular because there are many savers here in Japan and many people are complaining that they're not earning enough on their savings."
Economists said one of the main reasons for BOJ caution is uncertainty over the outlook for spending and capital investment after the consumption tax rise in April and a cut in government spending.
But there have been signs that the recovery is robust despite the jolt from the higher sales tax.

The Economic Planning Agency said last week it expected private machinery orders to rise a robust 4.5 percent in the April-June quarter from the previous quarter. Orders fell 7.0 percent in the January-March quarter, it said.

Meanwhile, an improvement in business sentiment has translated into higher market rates. JGB yields have been on an uptrend since the key 182nd JGB yield hit a record low 2.075 percent on April 8. -- Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-33432-8570
